title: CGI 2026 Must Know Session: Spending in 2026 — What Legal Operational Professionals Must Know (Ari Kaplan with Mark Ross, live from the CLOC Global Institute)
pub: CLOC Talk (Corporate Legal Operations Consortium) — recorded live at CLOC Global Institute 2026, Chicago; episode published 6 August 2026
author: Ari Kaplan · Mark Ross

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The exchange supports the cluster’s core account of buyer-driven work reallocation and pressure on inherited delivery economics. It describes clients bringing work in-house, expecting ALSPs to use AI, allocating outside counsel work according to expertise and judgment, and demanding efficiencies even where work remains external. Its evidence is qualitative and does not address the cluster’s verification or apprenticeship concerns.
qs: I'm definitely seeing a trend of in-house pulling work in, unquestionably an expectation that alternative legal services providers bring these technologies into their legal managed services that they're bringing to in-house counsel.
Clients are still expecting that they bring efficiencies to the delivery of that bucket of work that stays within the remit of outside counsel.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: The source supports the proposition that legal AI’s value depends on client-centred implementation rather than innovation alone. It prioritises partnership and transparency, while stressing accountability for mistakes as technology accelerates legal work.
qs: It's not being super innovative and transforming everything, it's being a partner.
If there's an error or a mistake, which there almost always has to be if you're moving quickly, own it, and work with me on how we better serve.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s view that AI is reallocating legal production rather than eliminating lawyers. It describes work being stratified among in-house teams, law firms and ALSPs, with technology handling suitable work while expertise, judgment and trust preserve a central role for outside counsel. It also supports buyer-driven efficiency and savings expectations while treating adoption as an ongoing transition.
qs: What you are really seeing now is an agreement on the stratification of work.
The law firm really should be doing this kind of work because of their expertise, because of their judgment, because of the trust we've placed in them, and where can we attack this together?

It also aligns with the cluster’s emphasis on client–provider workflow redesign and measuring value beyond isolated time savings, though its evidence is primarily qualitative and predictive.

kp.k: Clients and counsel seek equilibrium amid spending disruption
kp.d: Kaplan characterizes the 2026 market as disruptive but collaborative: clients still need law firms for risk management, talent and expertise. Reporting his panel with Hilton legal operations leader Alex Gao and Venable pricing head Julio Sanchez, he describes discussion of pricing's influence on team composition, alternative fees and reliance on alternative legal service providers. He reports Gao's view that outside-counsel financing is elevating legal operations' profile and Sanchez's account of firms seeking more creative client service; no quantitative spending findings are supplied.
qs: What I'm really seeing is that the clients and their counsel are very much trying to find some kind of equilibrium.

And the clients, while they recognize there's an evolution happening, need their law firms for risk management, for talent, for expertise, and they recognize that there needs to be a way through what's happening now.
And so we talked about things like how is pricing affecting who serves on which teams?
Are you using alternative fees? What is the extent to which you're trusting alternative legal services providers for certain kinds of projects?

kp.k: Conflicting AI policies complicate outside-counsel compliance
kp.d: Kaplan describes an exploratory phase over the preceding couple of years in which law-firm retainer letters and client outside-counsel guidelines could conflict over whether AI was permitted, including matter-specific permissions. He says compliance has been difficult but sees increasing outside-counsel sophistication and movement toward more settled arrangements. This is a qualitative account, without policy samples or compliance measurements.
qs: We've been seeing this exploratory phase over the last couple of years, uncertainty, outside counsel guidelines, and retainer letters kind of being out of sync where the law firm is saying, "Hey, we're using these tools."
Outside counsel guidelines saying, "We don't want you to use these tools," or, "You can use these tools on these types of matters."
It's very difficult to ensure compliance with where you're allowed to use these tools.
But we're settling now where outside counsel are increasingly sophisticated.

kp.k: AI encourages work allocation by comparative capability
kp.d: Kaplan sees emerging agreement on stratifying work: organizations can perform some tasks themselves with generative AI or other tools, retain law firms for expertise, judgment and trust, and collaborate on other work. He uses e-discovery as an analogy, describing a progression from law-firm advantage to client capability and eventually a shared understanding of which work belongs internally, with firms, with expert providers or with technology. This is his interpretation of market evolution, not a measured allocation of tasks.
qs: What you are really seeing now is an agreement on the stratification of work.
The law firm really should be doing this kind of work because of their expertise, because of their judgment, because of the trust we've placed in them, and where can we attack this together?
So again, real opportunity for collaboration, especially in areas where there's true understanding of who does what best.
where law firms had an advantage, and then clients really developed an advantage, and then they were both speaking the same language, and they can have a conversation, and that really normalized.

kp.k: Ross sees insourcing and pressure for tangible AI savings
kp.d: Host Mark Ross, rather than Kaplan, explicitly reports a trend toward in-house teams pulling work internally and expecting ALSPs to incorporate AI into managed legal services. He also argues that work retained by outside counsel remains subject to efficiency expectations, rather than permission to continue traditional delivery. Although he asks whether Kaplan's research supports this account, the transcript provides no quantified savings or insourcing results.
qs: I'm definitely seeing a trend of in-house pulling work in, unquestionably an expectation that alternative legal services providers bring these technologies into their legal managed services that they're bringing to in-house counsel.
But it's not a carte blanche for them to do that in the old traditional way.
Clients are still expecting that they bring efficiencies to the delivery of that bucket of work that stays within the remit of outside counsel.

kp.k: Kaplan emphasizes AI-enabled value rather than only cost reductions
kp.d: Responding to Ross's question about efficiency demands, Kaplan anticipates firms using AI to offer additional value previously unavailable or too time-consuming, and to better support clients' business success. He says clients remain willing to pay for essential legal services despite concern over expense, while competition among firms makes technology-enabled partnership a prospective competitive advantage. He does not provide measured price reductions or predict the replacement of hourly billing.
qs: Yes, I think that we are entering an era of law firms figuring out how to better delight their clients, and so finding ways to use these tools to add value that otherwise wasn't available or they didn't have time for, and be more thoughtful about the business and how some of their work could influence the trajectory of the success of their clients.
I mean, they ultimately are willing to pay for legal services.
So the competitive advantage is gonna be found in using the technology to be value-added providers, to be true partners.

kp.k: Provider relationships depend on transparency and accountability
kp.d: Kaplan invokes his annual eDiscovery Unfiltered report, which he says is in its 12th year, as qualitative support for the importance of fundamental provider traits rather than innovation alone. He identifies partnership, transparency and owning mistakes as recurring priorities and expects technology-driven speed to amplify their importance. No respondent counts, methods or numerical rankings are given.
qs: This is the 12th year that I'm publishing it.
And I always ask, "What are the qualities that matter most? When you're choosing a provider, working with a provider, what really matters most?"
And it's always fundamental traits. It's not being super innovative and transforming everything, it's being a partner.
Being transparent. If there's an error or a mistake, which there almost always has to be if you're moving quickly, own it, and work with me on how we better serve.
And that will just be amplified with technology, 'cause we're only working faster.

kp.k: Verification costs can undermine rapid AI drafting
kp.d: Kaplan describes his own experimentation with AI drafting and reports that many general counsel call the subsequent checking burden the 'validation tax.' His personal experience is that rapid generation can require extensive verification, leading him to prefer AI for organizing material and challenging or supplementing his thinking. This is an experiential account of augmentation, not a measured error rate or productivity study.
qs: Do I like when the tool drafts? I don't know that I like that, because then I ended up paying what a lot of general counsel call the validation tax.
I rapidly create something, and then I spend endless amounts of time making sure that what's been created is correct.
Instead, I have been trying to use it to organize, or as a sparring partner, as a peer who's capable of challenging me or highlighting some things that I think might be valuable to include.

kp.k: Legal operations careers require business skills and continuous experimentation
kp.d: Kaplan traces legal operations from an emerging chief-of-staff or law-department COO role discussed in his 2012 ACC Docket article, through an increasing technological focus including contract management, to the present importance of curiosity and tool experimentation. His recommendation combines business acumen, metrics, analytics, process design and partnership with thoughtful use of sophisticated tools to support the business; it does not frame technology skills as replacing the earlier foundations.
qs: I wrote an article about this emerging field in 2012.
It's called chief of staff or COO of the law department, and general counsel were starting to pull people with real estate talent or finance talent
It was so important to understand metrics and analytics, and to really be able to create processes around what was happening in the law department.
And I myself have been trying to use as many tools as I can to experiment.

that combination, not just of business acumen and of curiosity and of partnership, but also being thoughtful about where they're starting to leverage even more sophisticated tools to do more of the fundamentals of being partners and really responding and really supporting the business, that's where they'll shine.

kp.k: Demonstrating legal operations and AI returns remains difficult
kp.d: Kaplan reports that legal operations community members participating in his research struggle to demonstrate their contribution because much of it consists of cost avoidance. He urges scrutiny of returns on legal operations activity and technology investment, especially AI, and raises time to revenue alongside time savings as a possible focus. He says both law firms and corporations are beginning to consider these questions, without presenting an ROI methodology or investment-return results.
qs: The one challenge that I feel like a lot of members of this community have shared with me in my research is showing ROI of what legal operations leaders do has been challenging.
'Cause much of it is in cost avoidance.
What's the ROI of the investments that you're making in technology, especially in AI?
Is it just time savings? Is it now time to revenue? Where are the opportunities?
And you're starting to see companies really think about this on the law firm side and on the corporate side.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Ari Kaplan describes AI as reshaping work allocation, competitive differentiation and legal-operations practice, while creating verification costs that can offset drafting speed.
pts.d: Kaplan makes five connected claims. (1) After an exploratory period of inconsistent client and law-firm AI policies, increasing sophistication is enabling agreement on allocating work: corporate legal departments can perform some tasks themselves with generative AI, law firms retain work requiring expertise, judgment and trust, and some work invites collaboration. (2) Law firms will gain competitive advantage by using technology to add previously unavailable value and support clients' businesses, rather than simply performing existing services in the same way. His response emphasizes value and partnership; it does not quantify or independently establish the host's proposed hard-dollar savings trend. (3) Technology accelerates work and amplifies the importance of transparency, partnership and owning mistakes, with some disruption accompanying faster and better work. (4) In Kaplan's own experimentation, rapid AI drafting creates a substantial human verification burden, which he calls the 'validation tax'; he instead favors using AI for organization and as a sparring partner. (5) Legal-operations professionals who combine business acumen, curiosity, partnership and thoughtful use of sophisticated tools will be better positioned to demonstrate their abilities and support the business. He also observes growing attention to how AI investment returns should be measured, including whether benefits extend beyond time savings to time to revenue.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is qualitative research experience, professional observation, an analogy to e-discovery, and personal tool use—not quantified AI performance or savings results.
pts.d: For work allocation and policy convergence, Kaplan draws on his observations of the market and compares AI adoption with the earlier evolution of e-discovery, where firms and clients developed a shared understanding of what to handle internally or externally. For the importance of partnership and transparency, he cites recurring answers in his annual eDiscovery Unfiltered report, described as entering its twelfth year; these are provider-selection findings, not direct measurements of AI's competitive effects. His claim about drafting verification costs rests on personal experimentation, while the difficulty of demonstrating legal-operations ROI is attributed to community members participating in his research. He supplies no sample sizes, survey percentages, measured verification times, controlled comparisons, or AI-specific financial results. The predicted competitive benefits of value-added AI use and career benefits of curiosity and partnership are his interpretive judgments.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Kaplan places the transition in the present of the 2026 interview, following a couple of exploratory years, with open-ended predictions rather than dated milestones.
pts.d: The account describes AI policy and work allocation as currently becoming more settled, not as having reached universal equilibrium. Collaboration depends on understanding which participant performs which work best; law-firm retention of work is tied to expertise, judgment and trust. Competitive differentiation depends on actually using technology to add value and strengthen partnership, rather than adoption alone. The verification-cost qualification concerns Kaplan's experience of AI drafting and should not be generalized into a measured productivity result for all legal tasks. Career benefits are prospective and conditional on combining tool use with business acumen, curiosity and responsiveness. Questions about time savings and time to revenue identify emerging ROI considerations, not established revenue gains. No adoption deadline, savings target or timetable for replacement of lawyers is supplied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate legal departments, their outside law firms, and legal-operations professionals.
pts.d: Corporate legal departments can use AI to perform some work internally and collaborate with outside counsel on a more differentiated allocation of tasks, while continuing to purchase expertise and judgment. Law firms face peer competition and an opportunity to distinguish themselves through technology-enabled business value and stronger client relationships. Legal-operations professionals must navigate technology investment choices, demonstrate returns that can be difficult to distinguish from cost avoidance, and develop skills that connect tool use to business support. Users of AI drafting, illustrated by Kaplan himself, incur the human work of checking output before relying on it. The account concerns enterprise legal services; it does not offer concrete predictions about public access to justice, lawyer employment totals or associate staffing structures. Specific claims that clients demand ALSP technology adoption or hard-dollar savings are advanced by host Mark Ross and are not treated here as independent Kaplan findings.
